blocks.text: You can build websites - now let's build websites EVERYONE can use

You have learned tags, text, links, images, lists, tables, forms, semantics, modern HTML5. You CAN build complete websites and apps now. But can a blind person use your website? Can keyboard-only user navigate it? Will it load fast on slow Ghana mobile network? Will Google rank it? Today we cover what separates junior websites from professional production apps that serve millions.
Open Menu > Practical and open your complete webpage index.html from Lesson 8. We will audit and polish it to 95% production ready. Lesson 10 will be deployment.
Accessibility is not optional - it's law and it's humanity

Accessibility (a11y) means your complete website and apps can be used by people with disabilities - blind users with screen readers, deaf users needing captions, motor impairment users using keyboard only, color blind users. WCAG guidelines require: 1) Perceivable - alt text, captions, contrast. 2) Operable - keyboard navigation, skip links. 3) Understandable - labels, clear language. 4) Robust - valid HTML, ARIA when needed.

In many countries, inaccessible websites can be sued. But beyond law, think: if your client's customer is blind and can't order from their website because you didn't add alt or label, client loses money and you lose reputation. Professional complete websites and apps MUST be accessible.

blocks.text: Skip links, focus management and keyboard navigation

Keyboard users press Tab to navigate. If your website has 20 nav links, they must Tab 20 times on every page to reach main content. Skip link solves this: hidden link at very top that says Skip to main content, visible when focused, jumps to main. Also tabindex: tabindex="0" makes custom element focusable, tabindex="-1" makes it programmatically focusable but not in Tab order. Never use tabindex >0 - it breaks natural Tab order.

blocks.text: ARIA - when semantic HTML is not enough

First rule of ARIA: Don't use ARIA if semantic HTML can do it. Use button not div role=button. But sometimes you need ARIA: aria-label when visible text not descriptive enough, aria-labelledby to reference other element as label, aria-describedby for extra description, aria-required, aria-invalid for form validation, aria-expanded for collapsible, aria-hidden for hiding decorative. ARIA doesn't change behavior, only announces to assistive tech.

blocks.text: Performance - make your complete websites fast on slow networks

In Ghana, many users have slow 3G and expensive data. If your complete website and apps are heavy, they will leave. HTML performance tricks: loading="lazy" for images and iframes offscreen, width and height to prevent layout shift CLS, preload="metadata" for video not full video, link rel="preload" for critical resources, avoid too many iframes, optimize images with correct format jpg for photos, png for transparent, svg for icons/logos, webp modern best.

blocks.text: Validation, SEO and complete website launch checklist

Before you say your complete website and apps are done, validate: 1) W3C Validator - check HTML valid no errors. 2) Lighthouse - test Performance, Accessibility, Best Practices, SEO scores aim 90+. 3) Keyboard test - unplug mouse, Tab through entire website, can you access everything? 4) Screen reader test - use NVDA or VoiceOver, does it announce correctly? 5) Mobile test - does it work on phone with viewport?

blocks.question:
You have
Send
styled as button. It looks like button but keyboard user can't Tab to it or press Enter. Also screen reader doesn't announce as button. What are two critical fixes for accessible complete website?
options: Add style cursor:pointer to make it look more like button and add title="Send button" for screen readers

Fix 1: Add tabindex="0" to make it focusable and role="button" plus keydown handler for Enter/Space to make it operable by keyboard. Fix 2: Better yet replace div with semantic <button> which is natively focusable, operable, announced as button without extra ARIA or JS - semantic HTML first rule
Add alt="Send button" to div because div needs alt like img for accessibility

Wrap div in tag because a tags are keyboard accessible so
Send
 fixes keyboard issue
blocks.correctFeedback: Perfect! Semantic button > div role=button. This is core accessibility for complete apps.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Can div be focused by Tab by default? What role does screen reader announce for div?
blocks.reasoning: Div not focusable or announced as button by default. Button is natively accessible. If must use div, need tabindex, role, keyboard handlers - but semantic button is better.

blocks.question: You build complete website without skip link. Page has header with 15 nav links then main content. Keyboard user must press Tab 15 times on every page to reach main content. Why is skip link mandatory and where should it be placed?
options: Skip link is optional decoration, keyboard users can use mouse to skip nav, no need for skip link in complete websites

Skip link is mandatory for WCAG, must be first focusable element in body, hidden until focused, links to main content id, allows keyboard and screen reader users to bypass repetitive navigation and jump directly to main content saving 15 Tabs per page
Skip link should be at bottom of page after footer to skip back to top, not at top
Skip link should only be added with JavaScript because HTML cannot have skip links natively
blocks.correctFeedback: Excellent accessibility knowledge! Skip link is WCAG requirement for bypassing blocks.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Where would skip link be most useful? Top or bottom? For bypassing what?
blocks.reasoning: WCAG 2.4.1 Bypass Blocks requires mechanism to bypass repeated content. Skip link as first focusable element linking to main satisfies this.

blocks.question: You have email input without label, and image without alt on your complete website. Accessibility audit fails both. What is correct fix and why placeholder and missing alt fail?
options: Both pass, placeholder replaces label and images don't need alt if src is descriptive like team.jpg

Fix: Add label with for/id for email input because placeholder disappears on typing, low contrast, not reliably announced as label; add meaningful alt for informative image or empty alt for decorative - because screen readers need label to identify input purpose and alt to describe image content, without them blind users cannot use complete website
Fix: Add title attribute to both because title replaces label and alt for accessibility
Fix: Add aria-hidden="true" to both to hide them from screen readers and avoid audit failure
blocks.correctFeedback: Perfect! Label and alt are non-negotiable for accessible complete websites and apps.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: What happens to placeholder after typing? What does screen reader announce for image without alt?
blocks.reasoning: Label is persistent programmatic name, placeholder is hint only. Alt provides text alternative for images. Both mandatory for accessibility.

blocks.question: You use with empty alt for large hero image that shows text 'Welcome to My Portfolio' inside image. Lighthouse says accessible but blind user says they can't know what hero says. What is critical error?
options: Empty alt is always correct for large images, blind user is wrong, hero images should always have empty alt

Error is that image contains important text but alt is empty - empty alt is only for decorative images, if image conveys information or text, alt must describe that information. Also important text should not be inside image only - should be real HTML text over image for accessibility and SEO
Error is that hero image should have title not alt, so add title="Welcome to My Portfolio" and keep alt empty
Error is that hero image is too large, should be small icon with empty alt, text should be in separate div
blocks.correctFeedback: Excellent! Text in images is accessibility failure - use real HTML text.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Does empty alt mean decorative or informative? Where should important text live - inside image or as HTML?
blocks.reasoning: Empty alt = decorative, skip. Informative images need meaningful alt. Text inside images fails accessibility because screen readers can't read text in pixels, and not translatable or responsive.

blocks.question: You build complete website with no lang attribute on html, no width/height on images, no loading=lazy, and iframe without title. What are 4 impacts on complete website quality?
options: No impact, these attributes are optional and only for advanced developers, complete website works without them

Impact 1: No lang - screen readers use wrong pronunciation. Impact 2: No width/height - causes layout shift CLS hurting SEO and UX. Impact 3: No loading=lazy - loads all images immediately slowing page on slow networks. Impact 4: Iframe no title - fails accessibility audit, screen readers announce 'frame' without description - all hurt production quality of complete website and apps
Impact is only SEO, accessibility and performance are not affected by these attributes, only SEO ranking drops slightly
Impact is that website won't load at all without these attributes, browser blocks rendering until they are added
blocks.correctFeedback: Perfect production knowledge! These 4 attributes define professional vs amateur complete websites.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: What does lang do for pronunciation? What does width/height prevent? What does lazy do? What does iframe title provide?
blocks.reasoning: Lang = pronunciation, width/height = prevent CLS, loading=lazy = defer offscreen, iframe title = accessible name. All critical for production complete websites and apps.
